items.title: Interviewing Oscar Wilde's ONLY Grandson
items.description:
Oscar Wilde was a famous Victorian queer icon for his writing, for fame itself but also for his scandals. Merlin Holland has studied the life of his grandfather and is meeting with Anthony Delaney and Maddy Pelling to talk about Wilde's legacy, trials, affairs, prison and the impact on his family.

Subscribe to After Dark here: https://www.youtube.com/@AfterDarkHistoryHitsub_confirmation=1
Watch A Very Victorian Scandal here: https://youtu.be/xoHA3OAAf9E 

0:00 Introduction
1:40 Merlin Holland a
items.why_watch: Merlin Holland is the last living direct link to Oscar Wilde, and he's spent decades correcting the record on his grandfather's life, trials, and legacy — including family details that rarely surface in standard biographies. At nearly 72 minutes it's a commitment, but Holland's perspective is genuinely irreplaceable rather than just adjacent.

items.title: Histories of the Kings of Britain by Geoffrey of Monmouth - Book VII
items.description: The History of the Kings of Britain (Historia regum Britanniae), originally called De gestis Britonum (On the Deeds of the Britons), is a pseudohistorical account of British history, written around 1136 by Geoffrey of Monmouth. It chronicles the lives of the kings of the Britons over the course of two thousand years, beginning with the Trojans founding the British nation and continuing until the Anglo-Saxons assumed control of much of Britain around the 7th century. It is one of the central piec
items.why_watch: Book VII of Geoffrey of Monmouth's 12th-century chronicle is where the Arthurian mythology gets its most elaborate early scaffolding, including Merlin's prophecies. This is a clean audiobook-style reading suited for people who want the primary source rather than a modern retelling.

global_silver_linings.title: Experimental Drug Generates Immune Response Against Pancreatic Cancer in People at High Risk
global_silver_linings.snippet: Researchers at Johns Hopkins report that an experimental drug targeting one of the most common genetic drivers of pancreatic cancer was safe in humans, and generated durable immune responses aimed at preventing the cancer in people at high risk. Pancreatic cancer has one of the lowest survival rates of any form, and the developers believe […] The post Experimental Drug Generates Immune Response Against Pancreatic Cancer in People at High Risk appeared first on Good News Network .
global_silver_linings.reason: Pancreatic cancer is one of the hardest cancers to treat, so an experimental drug that successfully triggers an immune response in high-risk patients marks a genuinely significant step forward. Early promise like this can change survival odds for a disease that has long had very few options.

global_silver_linings.reason: The rediscovery of Kate Warne's remarkable story reminds us that courage and intelligence have always defied the expectations placed on people — and that history still holds inspiring figures waiting to be found. Her legacy is a quiet but powerful testament to what one determined person can accomplish.

global_silver_linings.title: Maternal RSV vaccine cuts newborn ICU admissions in half
global_silver_linings.snippet: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Good news! In the UK, only 63 infants were admitted to intensive care with RSV infection last winter, which is down from 131 the year before. Same 20 hospitals, same surveillance system.
global_silver_linings.reason: A vaccine given during pregnancy that cuts newborn ICU admissions from RSV in half is the kind of straightforward, life-saving win that medicine works hardest to achieve. For families with vulnerable newborns, this means fewer frightening first weeks and more babies going home healthy.

discovery_articles.title: The World’s Oldest Living Things: 14 Ancient Organisms
discovery_articles.snippet: All over the world, you can find ancient organisms that have existed for thousands, sometimes even millions, of years: living testaments of endurance and adaptation amidst changing climates and environmental degradation. Many of these organisms are trees—especially, massive, hulking ones whose branches burrow deep and widespread under the Earth. Others are clonal colonies: intricately designed natural systems in which an organism copies itself ad infinitum.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Some of the oldest living things on Earth aren't grand solitary elders but clonal colonies — organisms that have quietly been copying themselves for thousands of years, hiding their age in plain sight. A forest, it turns out, can be a single creature.

discovery_articles.title: Volvo Island in Ottawa, Illinois
discovery_articles.snippet: In 2012, the owner of a local Ottawa, Illinois, repair shop towed a 2001 Volvo S80 onto a peninsula and then used an excavator to create a small, one-car island. He intended to run a contest asking people to guess how the Volvo got there. The contest never materialized, as there was some concern that people might try to cross the 40-foot-deep lake for a better look.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: A man towed a Volvo onto a hand-dug island in 2012 just to run a guessing contest — and then never ran the contest, because he worried people might drown trying to cheat. The car is still there.

discovery_articles.title: ‘The Missing’ Cabin in Jemez Springs, New Mexico
discovery_articles.snippet: Located just off the main entrance road of New Mexico’s Valles Caldera–a 14-mile-wide circular depression created by a massive volcanic eruption 1.2 million years ago–it is hard to believe that this cabin could have gone missing. Instead, this cabin was built as part of the set of “The Missing,” a 2003 Western starring Tommy Lee Jones and Cate Blanchett. Since the National Park Service began managing the preserve in 2015, the scenic cabin has been left in place for visitors.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: A film set cabin built inside a 1.2-million-year-old volcanic crater was simply… left behind, and is now a legitimate landmark in a National Park. Hollywood's throwaway prop became a piece of accidental history.

discovery_articles.title: Isis Heiligtum (Isis and Magna Mater Temple) in Mainz, Germany
discovery_articles.snippet: What do you do when you've built a shopping mall but you find an ancient Roman temple underneath part of it? If you are in Mainz, Germany, you build the mall up around it, but leave it in place to be a hidden museum to the past. This is the "Isis-Heiligtum" (Isis Temple) in Mainz, Germany, preserved in place beneath the Römerpassage shopping mall within an easy 10-minute walk from Mainz Hauptbahnhof train station.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Beneath a busy shopping mall in Mainz, Germany, a Roman temple to Isis sits preserved and hushed — a secret museum that shoppers walk directly above without a second thought. The ancient and the mundane, separated by a ceiling.

discovery_articles.title: NASA-Funded Mission to Rescue a Falling Space Telescope Officially Ends in Failure
discovery_articles.snippet: The commercial LINK spacecraft was supposed to give NASA's Swift observatory a boost, pushing it higher into orbit to extend its life. But after launch, LINK experienced several problems. Swift is expected to re-enter Earth's atmosphere and burn up by the end of this year
discovery_articles.ferns_note: NASA's Swift telescope spent 20 years catching the universe's most violent explosions, and its final act will be a quiet, unglamorous burn-up over Earth's atmosphere — no rescue, no ceremony, just the end of a brilliant run.

discovery_articles.title: How Should the Bayeux Tapestry End? A New Competition Invites Children to Reimagine Its Missing Final Panel
discovery_articles.snippet: Some historians think the 230-foot-long artwork is missing its final panel, which may have once depicted William the Conqueror's coronation. As the tapestry goes on view in London, students will be drafting endings of their own
discovery_articles.ferns_note: The Bayeux Tapestry — 230 feet of embroidered conquest — may simply stop mid-story, its final panel lost to nine centuries of silence. Now children are being asked to finish what history couldn't.

discovery_articles.title: Narwhals Sport Iconic Straight, Spiraled Tusks. Scientists Just Uncovered Some of the Eye-Catching Feature's Structural Secrets
discovery_articles.snippet: The Arctic whales are the only known animals with straight tusks, and ones that consistently twist to the left. New research reveals that the inner layer twists to the right and that the opposing spirals provide strength and help the tusks grow straight
discovery_articles.ferns_note: The narwhal's tusk is the only straight tusk in nature, and it stays straight precisely because its inner and outer layers spiral in opposite directions — a quiet structural argument happening inside the bone all along.

discovery_articles.title: Construction in Austria Revealed a Roman-Era Mass Grave Beneath a Soccer Field. New Research Suggests That the Men's Enemies Targeted Their 'Sensitive Areas'
discovery_articles.snippet: No written records mention a fight in this specific part of Vienna at the time of the men's deaths. But the brutal nature of their injuries, particularly to the pelvis area, indicates that these individuals died on the battlefield
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Beneath a Vienna soccer field, Roman-era soldiers were found with injuries so deliberate and targeted that researchers could read the cruelty of their enemies in the bones themselves — no written record needed.

discovery_articles.title: Why Epstein-Barr is the ‘everything virus’
discovery_articles.snippet: The Epstein-Barr virus has taken a huge toll on global health. Understanding how it works could offer ways to combat multiple sclerosis, cancer and more.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Epstein-Barr is the virus most of us caught in childhood and promptly forgot — but it may be quietly linked to multiple sclerosis, several cancers, and a startling range of chronic diseases, making it one of the most consequential passengers the human body carries.

discovery_articles.title: ‘Stories in the Seams’ Showcases the Enduring Legacy of Black Quilts Across Centuries
discovery_articles.snippet: From 18th-century hand-appliqué cotton bedcovers to contemporary narrative textile works, Black quilts tell innumerable stories. discovery_articles.ferns_note: Black quilts have functioned as diary, protest, memory, and map across centuries — textile works that hid entire worlds in their seams long before anyone thought to hang them on a gallery wall.

news.title: When it comes to rosé, pink doesn’t have to mean Provence
news.snippet: From Morocco to Monmouth, there’s a whole world of blushing rosé wines to discover Hello, from rosé season, the only time of year I order wine like a patriarchal septuagenarian. For this fleeting moment in the wine-drinking calendar, questions are out and assumptions are in; everyone’s happy to drink pink – specifically, pale, dry and berry-crisp Provence rosé. Blushing like cheeks in a summer romance, pale rosé captures something of the hazy holiday spirit: easy, fun, objectively delicious.
news.blurb: A lovely reminder that the world of rosé stretches far beyond the sun-bleached hills of Provence, and your glass is all the richer for it.
